messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Taxi/Uber Driver
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 27-year-old African American man who has been driving for Uber and a local taxi company since his early twenties, preferring the long hours alone in his car to jobs that would put him under someone else’s supervision. In the first sessions he described growing up with a caregiver whose violence was sudden and bodily intimate: he would hear footsteps coming down the hall and feel his whole body lock before the person even entered the room. What stayed with him most was not a single blow but the sensory pattern around it—the scrape of footsteps behind him, the shock of temperature against his skin, and the feel of a particular rough household fabric that touched him during those episodes. He said those details still make his body react before his mind can catch up.

As an adult, those sensations break into ordinary moments with alarming force. A rider shifting in the back seat so that he hears footsteps as they approach his car from behind can make him grip the wheel and scan the mirrors. A blast of cold air from a passenger opening the door at night, or the brush of a seat cover or jacket with a texture that reminds him of childhood, can leave him instantly on guard. He does not experience reassurance as reassuring; even when a passenger is calm or a friend tells him he is fine, he cannot trust the feeling of safety. Instead he becomes superalert, tracking movements, watching hands, and bracing as if harm is about to happen. On bad nights he drives faster than he should, takes pickups in rough areas without thinking through the risk, and later recognizes that he has been acting as if danger is unavoidable anyway.

Over time, he has built his life around getting away from that surge. If a rider’s coat brushes him with the wrong texture, or cold rain soaks through his shirt at a pickup, he will turn up music, scroll his phone at stoplights, or look for anything to distract himself from what is happening inside him. After certain shifts he smokes or uses drugs because being numb feels easier than feeling ambushed by his own body. Emotional closeness has become another thing to avoid. He has ended promising relationships when partners wanted to know him more deeply, because the combination of being physically near someone and feeling watched inside his own skin is intolerable. The same footsteps and skin sensations that make him feel under threat push him toward distance, distraction, and drug use as the quickest exits he knows.

What gives these habits their grip is what he has come to believe about himself. Kwame says he has permanently changed for the worse, that whatever happened in childhood damaged something basic in him. When his chest tightens or his shoulders tense before he has consciously identified a sound or sensation, he takes it as proof that his body is now an enemy, reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is technically safe. He also speaks painfully about feeling cut off from his community and culture, as though other people move through family gatherings, church events, or neighborhood spaces with a belonging he no longer has. Because he sees himself as altered, cut off, and physiologically unreliable, withdrawing from intimacy and blotting himself out with distraction or drugs feels sensible to him, almost responsible.

Those beliefs also intensify the danger he feels in daily life. If his own body can betray him, then any spike of tension becomes evidence that a threat is real. He grows more watchful, more certain that safety cannot be trusted, and more likely to meet ordinary uncertainty with the readiness of someone expecting attack. That constant alertness, in turn, seems to sharpen the very cues he dreads. He notices footsteps behind him before anyone else would. He is acutely aware of cold air on his forearms when passengers enter the car. He reads textures against his skin with exaggerated precision. By the end of a long shift he can feel as though the world is full of these reminders.

The ways he copes leave him feeling even more estranged afterward. Turning away from partners confirms his sense that he has lost connection; getting high after work leaves him ashamed and more convinced that he is not the man he wanted to become. Even distraction carries a cost, because every time he has to scramble away from his own reactions he comes back to the same conclusion: something in him is broken and still living in that old house. In recent months his work has started to suffer. He has canceled rides abruptly, avoided lucrative airport pickups at dawn because of the cold, and nearly got into an altercation after a customer walked up behind him too quickly. He came to treatment after realizing he was organizing his whole life around not feeling what he feels. What frightens him most is that this is permanent—that he will never trust safety, never be close to anyone, and never get his body back. What he hopes, though cautiously, is that these reactions might finally stop running his life.
